Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

plotly.core 0.1.0

  • Initial CRAN submission.
  • Graph objects generated from the plotly.js (4.3.0) schema, with plotly.py-style validation and generated documentation: go_figure(), add_<trace>(), update_layout(), update_traces() and friends, and a go_*() constructor for every object in the schema, each with exactly that object’s properties (#5):
    • traces and the layout: go_scatter(), go_bar(), …, go_layout();
    • objects shared across the schema, one constructor for all of their places: go_font(), go_colorbar(), go_hoverlabel(), go_legendgrouptitle(), go_tickformatstop(), go_domain(), go_pattern() and go_error_bar() (plotly.js’s shared TypeScript types), go_bins(), go_minor(), go_rangebreak(), … (objects that are the same everywhere they appear), x/y/z axes that are the same (go_scene_axis(), go_ternary_axis(), go_caps_axis(), …), the selected/unselected point styles of all traces (go_selected(), go_unselected()) and the objects in them (go_colorbar_title(), go_selected_marker(), …);
    • every other object, named after its path without layout.: go_scatter_marker(), go_scatter_marker_line(), go_sankey_link(), go_xaxis(), go_scene(), go_scene_camera_eye(), go_annotation(), go_slider_step(), …, with go_layout_title(), go_layout_image(), go_layout_colorscale() and go_layout_transition() where the path name would be ambiguous or is a trace’s.
    Constructors take properties by name only (no positional arg; start from a list with do.call()), so names are never partially matched and unknown ones get an error that suggests the right name. Named lists work wherever an object does. One-sided formulas (go_scatter_marker(color = ~cyl)) are kept by constructors and evaluated in the data, then checked, when the trace is added with add_<trace>() or add_trace(). plotly.py’s “magic underscore” property names (marker_size = 10) are not supported.
  • Plotly Express (px_scatter(), px_bar(), …) is in the separate plotly.express package, which builds on plotly.core; plotly.core exports the functions it uses (see ?"plotly.core-extending"). plotly.py’s colour sequences and scales are plotly_colors. plotly.core no longer imports data.table (#4).
  • make_subplots(), templates (default_template(), register_template()); figures use no template ("none", plotly.js’s own defaults) unless one is set, as plotly 4.x does.
  • Figures rendered with the "none" default template have plotly 4.x’s margins (l = 60, r = 10, t = 25, b = 40 pixels) unless the layout sets them.
  • add_<trace>() takes data-driven defaults as plotly 4.x does:
    • split = ~col adds one trace per level, named after it;
    • colour properties given a discrete column (marker = go_scatter_marker(color = ~group)) split the same way, with viridis colours for ordered factors and the colorway otherwise;
    • axis titles, trace names and colorbar titles come from the formulas, and factor x/y values keep their level order, unless set.
  • add_annotation(), add_shape() and the other layout element functions take vectors for single-value properties, adding one object per element.
  • update_layout() has every layout property as an argument, documented in ?update_layout.
  • Colorscale names plotly.js knows ("Blues", "Viridis", …) use plotly.js’s definitions, as in plotly.js and plotly 4.x; others are plotly.py’s. With the "none" default template, colour scales default to viridis, as in plotly 4.x.
  • options(plotly.core.plotlyjs = "cdn") loads plotly.js from cdn.jsdelivr.net instead of copying it next to the HTML, e.g. for websites with many pages.
  • update_xaxes(), update_traces() and the other update_*() / select_*() functions accept vectors and "all" for row and col, as documented.
  • The pkgdown site has an Examples gallery: the Plotly R documentation examples rewritten with plotly.core graph objects.
  • htmlwidget rendering: numeric arrays are sent as base64 typed arrays, arrays repeated in a figure are sent once, as_float32() sends data in single precision, and partial_bundle() loads a smaller plotly.js bundle.
  • Numbers and date-times are sent without loss of precision: typed arrays carry doubles exactly, numbers in JSON are written in the fewest digits that read back as the same double, and date-times keep microseconds.
  • write_html() saves figures as HTML pages faster than htmlwidgets::saveWidget().
  • available_fonts() lists the font families installed on this computer (with the systemfonts package), and save_image() warns when a figure asks for a font that is not installed; see ?available_fonts for local versus viewer fonts.
  • Shiny (plotlyOutput(), renderPlotly(), event_data(), plotlyProxy()), knitr/Quarto output, and static image export (save_image()) to PNG, JPEG, WebP, SVG, PDF and EPS with headless Chrome via chromote, with LaTeX typeset by MathJax; no Python or Kaleido needed.
  • MathJax 3.2.2 (tex-svg.js) is bundled: config(mathjax = "local") (or TRUE) renders LaTeX (TeX()) offline and in self-contained HTML, and save_image() typesets it without network access. config(mathjax = "cdn") still loads it from cdn.jsdelivr.net.
  • save_image() sends figures to Chrome as the widget does: numeric arrays and date-times as base64 typed arrays, and arrays shared by traces once (decoded by the widget’s own code, lib/plotlycore/codec.js), so exports of large figures are several times faster than with Kaleido. Exports wait up to getOption("plotly.core.export_timeout", 300) seconds.
  • save_image() finds Chrome or another Chromium-based browser (Microsoft Edge, Chromium, Brave, including per-user installs), or offers to download Chrome Headless Shell in interactive sessions. On Linux it checks the shared libraries Chrome needs and can download missing ones into the user cache without administrator rights (Debian/Ubuntu and RHEL-family systems); install_chrome() does the same set-up non-interactively, and remove_chrome() removes the downloads. Startup failures show Chrome’s own output.
  • Renders the plotly R package’s plot_ly() and ggplotly() figures, including its crosstalk linking (highlight()).
  • Linked views with crosstalk: go_figure() and add_<trace>() accept a crosstalk::SharedData as the data for formulas (add_scatter(x = ~col)) and link the traces of its rows, set_crosstalk_keys() links the traces of any figure, and highlight() sets how selections are made and shown (the same options as the plotly package’s highlight()).

Developed by Matthew Summersgill, Carson Sievert, Chris Parmer.
